turns.t: Come in, do sit down. Before we begin, how would you like me to address you? Mr. Pemberton, or something more informal?
Mr. Pemberton is perfectly fine, thank you. Though my friends call me Alistair, if you prefer.
Mr. Pemberton it is, for now. Tell me what has brought you in this morning.
Well, I woke at about six and found my left arm and leg felt rather weak. Heavy, you might say. It was quite sudden, or rather, it was there as soon as I woke.
So you woke up with weakness down your left side. Did you notice it before you went to bed?
I did not. I was perfectly well last night. I watched the news and went up at ten.
Understood. How long has it been there now?
About three hours. It was worse when I first stood up. It has eased slightly since, but I would not say it has gone.
All right. So, weakness down the left side, there since you woke, and a little better but not gone. Have I got that right?
Exactly right, doctor.
Good. Has anything made it better or worse that you've noticed?
Not that I can say. I tried shaking the arm out, but that did not seem to change anything.
Fair enough. Now I need to ask about your speech. Any problem with your speech, finding words or slurring?
No. My wife says I sound entirely like myself, which she does not always mean as a compliment.
Ha. Then let me have a look at you. First, I'd like to look at your face. Could you smile for me, and show me your teeth?
Like this?
Lovely. Now raise your eyebrows, and close your eyes tightly.
Certainly. Is this all right?
Yes. Your face looks even on both sides. Now hold both arms out in front of you, palms up, and squeeze my fingers with each hand in turn.
I do notice the left one is a little slower to come up.
I can feel that you squeeze with both hands, and the strength in both arms is equal. Thank you.
Does that mean it is nothing at all?
What I can tell you is what I found. Your face is even, your arms are equal in strength, and your speech is normal. I'm not going to give it a name today, because I'd be guessing.
I would rather you be honest than reassure me for the sake of it.

Then here's the honest part. We watch it carefully. If any of these happen, you must not wait and see: your face drops on one side, your speech goes slurred or muddled, or the weakness gets worse. In that case you call 999 immediately.
Face, speech, weakness. I have seen the advertisement on television.
Exactly that one. And your wife should know it too, so she can act if you're not able to.
I shall tell her this evening. She will be rather pleased to have a job.
Good. Rest today, don't drive, and keep your phone within reach.
Not driving is no hardship. I am not very fond of the motorway anyway.
Then that is settled. Now, if it hasn't gone away within three days, I want you back here to see me, even if you feel it's improving.
If it has not gone in three days, I return. Understood.
Do ring the surgery in the morning to book that, so you're not waiting in a queue.
I shall. Is there anything else I should do in the meantime?
Plenty of water, a light lunch, and gentle movement of the arm and leg. No heavy lifting.
Gentle movement. Very good.
Do you have any questions for me before you go, Mr. Pemberton?
Only whether I should telephone my sister. She worries terribly.
Do ring her, and let her know the plan, so that someone else is aware of it too.
Thank you, doctor. I'm grateful for your time.
